races.summary: Two candidates, both printed as Democratic, are on the general ballot for the seat held by Nancy Pelosi, who is not on the ballot.
races.turns_on: How do the candidates' housing and local-transportation records and positions compare, and which matters to you?

evidence.text: Reported (Mission Local, Nov 20, 2025; date of the act not given): as District 1 Supervisor she attempted to pass amendments to "exempt existing housing stock" from the mayor's upzoning plan. Per the article, the amendments were not integrated because they "would have effectively gutted it and made it noncompliant with state requirements."
Per Mission Local, in January 2026 she was the first to sign a failed measure to reopen the Great Highway, and she backs Prop G.
Mission Local reports she opposed Proposition K (2024, removing cars from the Great Highway).
KQED reported on April 17, 2026 that she had raised about $456,000 (pre-primary); later periods not checked on the official FEC site.

Senator's office page: he authored SB 79 (Abundant and Affordable Homes Near Transit Act), signed Oct 10, 2025; it sets state height standards near major transit stops. Final vote counts differ across sources and were not confirmed on leginfo (blocked), so UNVERIFIED.
Per Mission Local, he opposes Prop G, authored the official argument against it in the voter pamphlet, and spoke at the No on G kickoff on Aug 16.
KQED reported on April 17, 2026 that he had raised nearly $3.5 million from over 3,300 donors (pre-primary); later periods not checked on the official FEC site.

races.summary: Two candidates, Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton, advanced from the June 2 top-two primary.
races.turns_on: Which candidate's stated plans on housing, taxes and homelessness, and track record in or out of office, match what you want the next governor to do?

evidence.text: As Attorney General he filed suit against Vitol, Inc. and SK Energy Americas alleging manipulation of California's gasoline market (Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law).
Campaign site says that as Attorney General he sued the Trump administration more than 120 times, and lists housing, homelessness, energy and AI among issues.

CalMatters guide: would declare a state of emergency to fund 40,000 units of already-approved affordable housing and "push cities to zone more residential land to build apartments, duplexes and condos."
CalMatters guide: he says people "should not be allowed to voluntarily stay on the street when offered shelter," but stopped short of saying they should face arrest.
At the Sept 30 debate he opposed Hilton's income-tax plan; CalMatters guide says he backs extending higher rates on high earners for schools.
Capitol Weekly: mid-year cash on hand $6.2 million; $6 million raised since July 1 in large donations.
No prior elected office; CalMatters lists background as former U.K. prime minister adviser, Silicon Valley entrepreneur and former Fox News host (2017-2023). No voting record to cite.
At the Sept 30 debate he said he would eliminate state income taxes on the first $150,000 of earnings; CalMatters guide also lists halving the gas tax.
CalMatters guide: street camping should be illegal and police should clear encampments; fund sober housing.
At the Sept 30 debate he advocated building 10 new cities and expanding construction on undeveloped land.
Capitol Weekly: mid-year cash on hand $2.1 million, with $1.4 million in unpaid bills; $1.2 million raised since July 1 in large donations; spokesman said he has more than 100,000 donors.

races.race: State Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers)
races.summary: Initiative constitutional amendment and statute that would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on net worth over $1 billion for California residents as of Jan 1, 2026.
races.turns_on: Whether a one-time wealth tax on billionaires, with 90% of revenue for health care, is worth the uncertain revenue and the possible loss of some ongoing income-tax revenue.
races.yes_means: YES: billionaires who were California residents on Jan 1, 2026 would owe a one-time tax of up to 5% of net worth, due in 2027 (payable over five years at extra cost); 90% of revenue for health care, 10% for education or food assistance. https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-title-summ-analysis.pdf
races.no_means: NO: no wealth tax is imposed and current tax law is unchanged. https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-title-summ-analysis.pdf
races.fiscal: Legislative Analyst: temporary revenue increase probably in the tens of billions of dollars over several years, very hard to predict; possible ongoing income-tax decrease of less than $1 billion per year; administration costs possibly tens of millions per year. If Prop 41 or 42 gets more yes votes, courts could find a conflict that blocks Prop 40. https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-title-summ-analysis.pdf

for.text: Argument in official guide (as summarized): the tax addresses federal health-care funding cuts. Supporters include SEIU United Healthcare Workers West and Sen. Bernie Sanders; support committees total $31,411,525 through Aug 2, 2026.

against.text: Argument in official guide (as summarized): it is a flawed one-time scheme that hurts the economy and does not lower health-care costs. Opponents include California Teachers Association and California Medical Association; opposition committees total $11,270,000 through Aug 2, 2026.

evidence.text: Support committees reported $31,411,525 and opposition committees $11,270,000 through Aug 2, 2026 (Secretary of State).
Official Legislative Analyst estimate: tens of billions in temporary revenue; possible ongoing income-tax loss under $1 billion per year.

races.race: San Francisco Proposition H (Parcel Tax to Fund Public Muni Operations)
races.summary: Ordinance that would create a new annual parcel tax from July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2042 to fund Muni service.
races.turns_on: Whether a new parcel tax is the right way to fund Muni operations, compared with possible service cuts and other funding sources.
races.yes_means: YES: the City funds Muni service through a new annual parcel tax (2027 base tax $129 single-family, $249 multifamily, $799 non-residential, plus square-footage rates; inflation-adjusted; many seniors discounted or exempt; up to 50% pass-through to rent-controlled tenants capped at $65 per unit per year). https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/Final_Digest_-_Parcel_Tax_to_Fund_Muni_Operations.pdf
races.no_means: NO: no parcel tax is created; Muni keeps its current funding sources. https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/Final_Digest_-_Parcel_Tax_to_Fund_Muni_Operations.pdf
races.fiscal: City Controller economic impact report: tax would generate $184 million per year; Controller estimates 800 to 1,445 additional jobs and $310 to $400 million in GDP on average over 15 years versus a scenario with service cuts. This is an economic impact report, not the pamphlet Controller's statement, which was not read. https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/MUNI_parcel_tax_economic_impact_final.pdf

for.text: Official proponent argument (Mayor Daniel Lurie and others): Muni is a lifeline for workers, seniors and students; without Prop H service could be cut by 30% and at least 20 bus routes eliminated; the tax funds only Muni service, with oversight and independent audits.

against.text: Official opponent argument (San Francisco Republican Party): the 15-year tax has no binding cost-cutting or efficiency requirements and no results-based sunset; the efficiency review comes in April 2028, after collection starts, and reports only to SFMTA's board; a square-footage tax is flat rather than value-based, and landlords can pass part of it to tenants.

evidence.text: City Controller report: $184 million annual revenue; 800 to 1,445 jobs and $310 to $400 million GDP over 15 years relative to the cuts scenario.
Yes committee raised $3.5 million as of end of June, with $500,000 each from OpenAI, Anthropic, Airbnb and Ripple Labs (Mission Local). No opposition committee total was found.
